Never miss what you actually buy

Add the items your household or workplace looks for. When a store tags one, it is held for the people who asked first. Finding a deal stops being luck and starts being a list.

Fridge Rescue

Tell Save4Good what is already in your fridge and close to its date. Fridge Rescue matches it with a ready item or a short list from the board, so what you already paid for gets used first, in a real meal, tonight.

Example combination: half a rotisserie chicken + frozen vegetables from the board. Package sizes and servings are not verified here — check quantities before planning a meal around it.

Family Essentials Boxes

A box with its full contents listed before you pay. No mystery, no surprise bag. Staples and household essentials recovered from grocery non-food stock, at one clear price.

Example contents, listed in full: diapers, soap, laundry detergent, rice, canned vegetables, and toilet paper. The exact list is shown on every box.

SNAP / WIC information note: Some grocery items may be eligible under SNAP or WIC when you pay at the store register. This board gives information only. Eligibility is decided at the register, by the store and the program rules, not by Save4Good. Listings show the information so a family can plan before they travel.

The cause, in dollars

Unsold is not worthless. It is money already spent, waiting to be recovered.

A store has already paid for the product, the shelf space, the staff time and the refrigeration. When an item is thrown out, all of that is lost at once. When it sells at a markdown, most of it comes back.

Cleared at zero

Dead inventory, stock that stopped moving, is written off and discarded. Its recovery value today is $0, plus the cost of hauling it away.

Found by luck

Markdowns sell only to whoever happens to walk past the right shelf on the right day. Everyone else never learns the item existed.

Tossed at close

Ready meals made that morning are at their best for hours, then they are waste. The demand for them, at half price, is standing in line at other counters.

What could one grocery store recover?

Stores keep the full sale. The customer is theirs, the money is theirs, the goods never leave their building until the buyer picks them up.

Recovered at the register, monthly$2,000
Recovered over a year$24,000
Meals and goods kept in use, monthly≈ 500 items

Illustrative estimate from the two figures you set, at an average recovered item value of $4. It is not a result. Your own two-week free test replaces estimates with your store's real numbers, on one proof page.

How it works

One tag. One claim. One page of proof.

1

The tag is the listing

Staff mark an item down the way they already do. In the pilot, the listing goes up from that same markdown round, with the claim code on the tag. Once a store group connects its system, the tag's print posts the listing by itself. No extra scan, no extra task per item, in either shape.

2

Demand is already waiting

Families with want lists, verified lot buyers behind the private door, employers and institutions see the exact item, price and pickup window, and claim it. What does not sell to people routes to donation partners, then compost, in that order.

3

Every item is accounted for

Each month the store gets one proof page: pounds recovered, dollars recovered, and where every item went. The same page is the record a county or a funder can read.

The evidence chain, on every item

  1. Claim recordedCode, item, price and pickup window.
  2. Pickup confirmedThe store confirms the item left with the claimant.
  3. Recipient confirmedFor donations and lots, the receiving organization or buyer confirms receipt.
  4. Destination recordedHousehold sale, B2B sale, donation, or compost. Nothing leaves the record blank.
  5. Monthly proof pageAll four steps roll up into the one page the business and the county read.

Phase 1 · The whole focus

One door in Phase 1. Grocery stores only.

Phase 1 keeps the moving pieces small and local: independent and regional grocery stores in Wyandotte County. Food, non-food items and ready meals, all through the one grocery door. Small and local first, because the decision maker is in the building.

The grocery door — food, non-food and ready meals

  • Ready meals and prepared food. Deli and kitchen items made today, listed the moment they are marked down, claimed before close. This includes the employer lunch door below.
  • Dead inventory, food. Fresh, bakery, dairy, frozen and shelf-stable stock that stopped moving: seasonal goods, overstock, packaging changes, slow lines, and short dates, with the reason shown on every listing.
  • Dead inventory, non-food. Household essentials, personal care, cleaning, baby items and seasonal goods from the same store, listed plainly on the same board.
  • Frozen food, in full. Frozen meals, vegetables and staples are a named Phase 1 category, with honest dates and quantities.
  • Infant formula, with checks. Sealed only. Seal, date and lot are checked and recorded before a listing goes up. If any check fails, the item is not listed.
  • Dead cooked inventory for workplaces. Prepared food that would be tossed at close is offered first to employer shifts through pre-orders, at the price on the board.

Phase 2 · Later, by design

Hotels and pharmacies join in Phase 2

  • Pharmacies. Front-of-store dead inventory: vitamins, personal care, baby and household essentials. Phase 2, not the pilot.
  • Hotels. Hotel food, amenities, linens and the Hospitality Recovery Assessment, through the Ecotel service line. Phase 2.
  • Restaurants. Prepared food beyond the grocery kitchen. Phase 2.

Nothing is dropped. It is sequenced, so the pilot proves itself on grocery numbers first.

Business consulting · A named service

The Waste Lab

Save4Good's consulting and training service for grocery businesses. It finds where value is lost inside the store, fixes the routine that loses it, and trains staff to hold the fix. The board recovers value at the shelf. The Waste Lab reduces how much value reaches the markdown shelf at a loss in the first place.

1

Identify

Walk the store and the records. Name the categories, aisles and routines where value is written off.

2

Analyze

Root-cause review. Ordering, rotation, production quantities and markdown timing, checked against the write-off record.

3

Improve and Train

Change the routine, then train and onboard staff on it, with an introductory staff-support period while the new routine settles.

4

Recover Value

What still reaches markdown goes through the board, the private B2B lane, donation routing and compost, in that order.

5

Measure and Recognize

The monthly proof page measures it. Stores that hold the standard receive Save4Good recognition, recorded below.

What a store receives

  • An operations diagnostic of the store's write-offs, by category and by cause.
  • A root-cause review, in writing, with the changes ranked by recovered value.
  • Staff training and onboarding on the new routines, delivered in the store.
  • An introductory staff-support period, so questions are answered while the routine is new.
  • A weekly overproduction note for prepared food: what was made, what sold, what was left, and the quantity to make next week.

Entry product · Phase 1

The Grocery Recovery Assessment

One store. One review of its write-off record, its markdown routine and its prepared-food production. The store receives the findings, the ranked changes, and its first proof-page format. It is the first step before the free two-week board test, or on its own.

Recognition, stated plainly: stores that complete the loop and hold the standard are listed in the public recovery directory with Save4Good recognition of their recovery practice. It is a Save4Good network record. It is not a state certification, and it is never presented as one.

The full feature set

Every feature in Phase 1, in one place

Every feature exists for one reason: more of what a store already paid for ends up sold, used and counted, and less of it ends up thrown away.

Tag-trigger listing

The markdown tag and the online listing are one event. Staff work does not change, so the board stays live on the busiest day.

Exact items, claim codes

Real products, real prices, real quantities, with a code that holds the item for pickup. No mystery bags, no guessing, no wasted trips.

Why-available label

Every listing states why it is available: short date, overstock, made today, packaging change. A family decides with the full fact in front of them.

Dietary filters

Filter the board by halal, vegetarian, high protein and gluten-free notes, plus allergen information where the store provides it. Set once, applied to every listing.

Budget-first search

Sort the board by lowest price first, and search inside a budget. Affordable items are easy to find, listed plainly, never labelled by who is buying.

Want lists and alerts

Households and institutions register what they need. When it is tagged anywhere in the network, they hear first. Demand is known before supply moves.

Household savings tracker

A running monthly total of what the board saved a household against full price, built from its own claims. Savings a family can see and plan with.

Fridge Rescue

Food already at home, close to its date, matched with board items to make a real meal first. What a family already paid for gets used before anything new is bought.

Family Essentials Boxes

Recovered staples and household essentials in one box, with the full contents listed before payment. Exact, plain, and priced once.

SNAP / WIC information

Listings carry eligibility information where it applies. Information only: the store register and program rules decide, and the note says so.

Private B2B lane

Bulk lots sit behind a closed door for verified businesses only, with offers, counteroffers and private clearance rooms. Never on the public board.

The employer door

Workplaces pre-order ready meals for their teams at board prices. A Lunch Test Day proves it on one shift: employees pay, the store sells, nobody guesses.

Institutions as purchasers

Schools, senior homes, daycares and shelters post demand requests and buy in bulk through the network, at recorded prices. They are buyers, not only donation recipients.

Donation routing

What does not sell is offered to community organizations through the same system, and only what cannot be used goes to compost. Every route is recorded.

Local pickup helpers

Qualified local providers, booked for specific pickup and delivery runs, handle physical movement when a store or buyer needs it. Save4Good coordinates. The work stays local and paid per run.

Evidence chain

Claim, pickup confirmation, recipient confirmation and recorded destination on every item. If it is not confirmed, it is not counted.

The monthly proof page

One page per business per month: pounds recovered, dollars recovered or saved, and where every item went. It is what businesses pay for, and what government reads.

Public recovery directory

Every participating store, buyer, institution and recognized business is listed in one local directory, so the network is visible, trusted and easy to join.

The private B2B lane · Closed door

Bulk value moves privately. It is never posted in public.

Dead stock in quantity is not a public listing. It sits in the private lane, open to verified businesses only, where a store and a buyer can deal directly and quietly.

  • Verified businesses only. Every buyer and seller in the lane is checked before access is given.
  • Private clearance rooms: a store can offer a lot to selected buyers, not to the whole board.
  • Offers and counteroffers, in writing, inside the lane. The agreed price is the recorded price.
  • Institutions post demand requests here: the item, the quantity, the date needed. Stores and lot holders answer with offers.
  • What does not sell in the lane routes onward: donation partners first, then compost, recorded the same way.

For grocery businesses

We support your business along the way. That is the model.

Save4Good coordinates. Your store keeps its goods, its customers and its sale. Qualified local providers handle any physical work. We bring the demand, the board, the private lane, the Waste Lab and the record.

  • A two-week test, free, on your real shelves: half listed, half not, scored from your own numbers.
  • Nothing changes in your systems and no new work per item for your staff.
  • You are paid on what sells because of the claims. Stock heading to zero cannot lose money.
  • New customers walk in for a claimed item and shop the rest of your store on the way out.
  • Waste Lab training and support while the new routines settle, and your recovery record documented monthly.

How the pilot opens

Demand first. County second. Stores third.

Save4Good does not walk into a store with an idea. It walks in with named buyers already waiting and a county that already knows the record exists.

1

Find the demand

Employers, senior homes, schools, daycares, shelters and community organizations join the demand book first, with what they need, in writing. Institutions join as purchasers, with demand requests of their own.

2

Bring in the county

Wyandotte County leaders hear about the pilot while it is being built, through the Unified Government, so the impact record starts with public trust behind it.

3

Then the first store test

One local grocery store runs the free two-week test with a line of demand already behind it. The results land on the first real proof page.

Join the Wyandotte pilot

Whichever side of the shelf you stand on, there is a place for you.

Grocery stores join for the free test and the Grocery Recovery Assessment. Employers and institutions join the demand book as purchasers. Verified businesses request the private B2B lane. Local providers join the pickup helper list. County and community partners join the record. Tell us who you are and what you need, and we will prepare your introduction message, ready to send.

Recovering today's value for tomorrow's stronger community.
